analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own a handgun or semiautomatic rifle and logs every sale.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since its June 2026 introduction, with zero cosponsors and no scheduled action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone who owns a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that takes a detachable magazine to hold a federal firearm owner license, issued after rolled-fingerprint background checks, with a fee capped at $10 and renewal every five years. Every sale or transfer of those guns would have to run through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the transaction to a federal record-of-sale system. It also adds rules to report lost or stolen guns within 72 hours, penalize adults who leave guns accessible to children, and fund federal research on gun injuries. It has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun violence. The bill's findings cite 44,000 U.S. gun deaths in 2024, with Black children and teens 16 times and Latino children and teens 3 times more likely than White counterparts to die of gun violence, and state the purpose of keeping guns from people prohibited by law and helping police trace crime guns. Specifically, it would close the private-sale gap: today a person who is legally barred from buying a gun can buy one from a private seller with no background check; under this bill every sale of a handgun or detachable-magazine semiautomatic rifle would go through a licensed dealer who confirms the buyer holds a valid license.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to possess a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that accepts a detachable magazine without a federal firearm owner license, issued only after a fingerprint-based nationwide criminal background check by the Attorney General.

Requires every sale or transfer of those firearms to go through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license with the Attorney General and records a tracking number, ending unlicensed private sales of those guns.
Creates a federal record of sale system in which dealers report each covered transfer within 14 days, giving law enforcement a chain of custody for tracing guns used in crime.

Makes it a crime to fail to report a lost or stolen qualifying firearm within 72 hours, and creates a child access prevention offense punishable by up to 5 years when a child gets an unsecured gun and someone is killed or seriously hurt.
Lets states with licensing and record-of-sale systems meeting the federal standards get certified by the Attorney General, so their residents can rely on state licenses instead.

Directs the Attorney General to run a firearm injury research clearinghouse and study 'smart gun' technology, and sets out the bill's findings: 44,000 gun deaths in 2024 and more than 750 school shootings since Sandy Hook.

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners and the firearms trade. Tens of millions of people who own handguns or semiautomatic rifles would have to apply for a license with rolled fingerprints, a photograph, and mental-health disclosures, renew it every five years, and face up to 10 years in prison for possessing a covered gun without one. Dealers and manufacturers would take on new record-keeping, reporting, and inspection duties, and the bill repeals the current federal statute that prohibits the Attorney General from establishing a firearms registration system, replacing it with a mandatory record of every covered sale. Gun rights organizations have historically opposed federal licensing on these grounds; that opposition is not in the record for this bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes the existing federal prohibition on establishing a system of firearms registration and directs the Attorney General to build a record-of-sale database covering every sale of covered guns, even while another section states that nothing in the bill authorizes a national firearms registry — a tension critics would read as a de facto registry of gun owners and their weapons.

It creates new federal crimes carrying up to 10 years in prison for unlicensed possession of a covered gun, and makes it a crime to fail to report a change of address within 60 days or a lost or stolen gun within 72 hours, exposing ordinary owners to felony liability for paperwork failures.

Applicants must pay a fee, submit rolled fingerprints, disclose any past mental-health facility stay within five years, and, for applicants under 21, obtain written parental consent — and anyone denied or revoked must surrender their license and move any covered guns out of their control within 48 hours, with the denial reported to their local sheriff.

The hunting exemption only applies while the hunter is accompanied by a licensed person, and the licensing and transfer requirements would impose recurring costs and compliance work on small gun dealers in particular.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety case is real: universal licensing and dealer-recorded transfers would close the private-sale loophole for the guns most used in homicides, and the theft-reporting and safe-storage provisions address documented pathways from legal sale to crime gun. But the bill is broad — it covers the handguns and common semiautomatic rifles owned by tens of millions of Americans — and it pairs that scope with heavy criminal penalties, a mandatory federal transaction database created by repealing the existing anti-registry statute, and lifetime obligations (renewals, address reporting, loss reporting) that fall on every owner. The honest weighing: a substantial safety gain purchased with a significant, permanent expansion of federal control over a widely exercised activity, with the registry question being the most contested design choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 24, 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no scheduled action.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on June 24, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No senator from either party has signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action has been taken since the referral to the Judiciary Committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill simply has not moved. If it dies in committee without a vote, the people better off will be opponents of federal gun licensing and the firearms industry, which would avoid the new licensing, reporting, and inspection requirements entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of federal gun licensing, so far

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Blair Holt Firearm Owner Licensing and Record of Sale Act of 2026 in the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The bill has sat in the committee he chairs since referral with no hearing, markup, or floor action scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no senator of either party has cosponsored the bill [S3]; the only supporter on record is its Democratic sponsor, and the Republican-led committee has taken no action [S4].

industries.note: The bill makes dealers the mandatory middleman for every private sale of a covered gun, guaranteeing them transfer business and fees, but also saddles them with license verification, 14-day transaction reporting, records inspection, and criminal exposure for paperwork failures.

The bill requires manufacturers to submit production and sales figures to the Attorney General, adds inspection authority, and a licensing gate on handgun and semiautomatic rifle ownership could shrink the customer base for their best-selling products; the industry's interest in avoiding these rules runs against the public-safety purpose of the bill.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, a Senate Republican majority, and no committee action since referral, the bill is very likely to sit in the Judiciary Committee without a vote until this Congress ends — the same fate that met earlier versions of the Blair Holt licensing bill introduced in previous Congresses.
